summary: This Geology.com article explains shale, the most abundant sedimentary rock, as a fine-grained, laminated and fissile mudstone formed from compacted clay and silt. It covers shale's uses in oil and gas production (conventional and unconventional reservoirs, horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing), its use in brick, tile, clay and cement, and its composition and colors. It also addresses shale's hydraulic properties, the engineering problems of expansive soils and landslides, and how shale forms in sedimentary environments, including on Mars.
one_line: Geology.com overview of shale: a fissile, clay-rich sedimentary rock tied to oil and gas, building materials, expansive soils and landslides.
key_facts: Shale is the most abundant sedimentary rock and is found in sedimentary basins worldwide.
Shale is a fine-grained sedimentary rock that forms from the compaction of silt and clay-size mineral particles, commonly called mud, and is classified as a mudstone.
Shale is distinguished from other mudstones because it is fissile and laminated.
Black organic shales are the source rock for many of the world's most important oil and natural gas deposits.
The Barnett Shale of Texas was the first major natural gas field developed in a shale reservoir rock.

Horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing revolutionized drilling technology and paved the way for giant gas fields including the Marcellus Shale in the Appalachians, the Haynesville Shale in Louisiana, and the Fayetteville Shale in Arkansas.
The article states that these enormous shale reservoirs hold enough natural gas to serve all of the United States' needs for twenty years or more.
Mixing finely ground shale with water produces a clay that often has similar or superior properties to natural clay, which had been depleted by heavy use.
Cement is often made by heating crushed limestone and shale, which breaks down the limestone into calcium oxide and carbon dioxide.
Oil shale contains solid kerogen, with up to 1/3 of the rock being solid organic material.
Shale is defined as a laminated rock consisting of at least 67% clay minerals.
A black color in sedimentary rocks almost always indicates the presence of organic materials, and just one or two percent organic materials can impart a dark gray or black color.
Hematite can produce a red shale, while limonite or goethite can produce a yellow or brown shale.
Shale can serve as a cap rock for oil and natural gas traps and is an aquiclude that blocks or limits the flow of groundwater.
Expansive soils change volume as they wet and dry, and they are one of the most common causes of foundation damage to buildings in the United States.
Shale is the rock most often associated with landslides, because weathering transforms it into a clay-rich soil with very low shear strength, especially when wet.
